extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, media scholars and development practitioners interested in climate change communication and media influence
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing media coverage of climate change
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic analysis and evaluation of how mass media report climate change (mitigation and adaptation), including quantity, frames, sources, formats, and effects on public opinion and policy across national contexts. Suited for comparative content analysis and policy-relevant media studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Track the quantity of 'climate change' or 'global warming' coverage in newspapers and other media over time (counts, spikes, comparative trends across outlets and countries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longitudinal counts (e.g., articles per period) to identify discursive phases and link surges to events (IPCC reports, UNFCCC, Kyoto, films like An Inconvenient Truth). Note: 'more is not necessarily better' — quantity helps identify attention cycles but does not alone indicate quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing (selection and salience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how media 'frames' climate change: selection of aspects of perceived reality to make them more salient, which privileges certain problem definitions and interpretations (Entman: 'to frame is to select some aspects...and make them more salient').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify dominant frames (conflict, catastrophe, economic, moral, solutions, personalization) and analyze how structural and agential factors produce and reproduce those frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources cited / source legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Who gets cited as legitimate sources in stories (scientists, government officials, industry, NGOs, contrarians)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure frequency and prominence of source types; note shifts over time (e.g., government officials surpassing scientists in citations in some periods) and implications for accuracy and policy narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and false equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate journalistic practices of 'balance' that may give disproportionate attention to contrarian views and create misleading equivalence between scientific consensus and dissent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify instances where norms of balance amplify minority or industry-funded 'sceptic' claims; assess impacts on public understanding and policy paralysis (Boykoff & Boykoff findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on mitigation versus adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the topical focus of coverage (mitigation of emissions vs adaptation to climate change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify proportion of pieces addressing adaptation (historically low; e.g., <1% in 1988-1990 in examined US/UK press) versus mitigation, and analyze implications for policy agendas and aid for vulnerable countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate story prominence: headlines, page placement, section (News, Business, Entertainment), column inches, and broadcast airtime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use placement and sectioning as indicators of salience and audience reach; note cross-section diffusion (e.g., climate stories appearing in Entertainment/Style broaden audience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and news hooks / event-driven coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how external events (IPCC reports, scientific testimony, extreme weather, policy conferences, films, celebrity actions, court cases) function as 'news hooks' that trigger coverage spikes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link temporal coverage spikes to specific events (e.g., Hansen testimony 1988; Gore film; Stern Review; COP meetings) to understand drivers of attention and agenda-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic norms, constraints and routines
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for micro-level journalistic factors (time/space pressures, beats, training, norms to inform rather than educate) that shape coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine newsroom constraints (column inches, time-management across beats) and their interaction with macro pressures to explain content choices and omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro political-economic influences (ownership, profit motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how media ownership structures, market pressures, advertising, corporate consolidation, and profit-seeking influence news production and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider size of firm, horizontal/vertical integration, advertiser influence and owners' interests (McChesney/Herman & Chomsky frameworks) when explaining frame selection and story emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and reporting of scientific uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how uncertainty in climate science is represented — whether it is contextualized, exaggerated, downplayed, or turned into paralyzing ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reporter practices in translating scientific uncertainty to public audiences; identify whether uncertainty is used to justify inaction or to emphasize caution; examine scientists' communication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of climate 'contrarians' and industry-funded voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the role and prominence of climate sceptics/contrarians, often funded by carbon-based industry interests, in media debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track funding linkages, citation frequency, and rhetorical strategies of contrarians; evaluate effects on politicization and public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and national context differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare national/regional differences in coverage (e.g., French emphasis on international relations, German portrayal as catastrophe, U.S. conflict framing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize frames within domestic political cultures, media systems, and institutional environments; avoid assuming uniform global framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium and format differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate coverage by medium (newspapers, television, radio, internet) and format (news, features, opinion, arts), noting reach and affordances (e.g., radio's importance in rural/developing contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select appropriate measures for each medium (audience share, airtime, frequency, program type); in developing countries, prioritize radio analyses where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratives, metaphors and storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the use of narratives, metaphors (e.g., 'greenhouse'), moral stories, and allusions that shape public meaning of climate change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring storylines and their implications for perceived responsibility, urgency, and feasible solutions; assess whether narratives promote action or fatalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization and celebrity/personal stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess use of personalized stories, celebrity endorsements, and individualized narratives to humanize or popularize climate issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure frequency and placement of personalized/celebrity stories (e.g., Richard Branson, Al Gore) and their effect on widening issue salience across sections and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual and performative representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate role of visual media, films, performance art, plays, and poetry in communicating climate change themes and shaping public engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include analyses of film releases, documentaries, and arts coverage as part of media ecology that influences mainstream news narratives and public affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional/affective engagement and public demobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how coverage affects public feelings (hopelessness, isolation, powerlessness) and levels of engagement or demobilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure presence of affective cues and messages about efficacy; consider trust in government and perceived agency as mediators of behavioral responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and translation of scientific findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate fidelity of media translations of scientific research into policy-relevant claims; identify 'mis-translations' or simplifications that diverge from science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare media claims with original scientific reports (IPCC etc.); check for loss of nuance, misreporting of causal claims, or inappropriate extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of vulnerable populations and equity/aid framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether and how media coverage addresses impacts on poor nations, adaptation funding needs, and questions of climate justice (who bears costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track narratives linking climate impacts to development assistance, quantify coverage about adaptation aid, and assess whether coverage mobilizes or obscures calls for international assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy salience and media influence on funding/aid
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess evidence that media reporting (especially disaster coverage) influences agency budgeting, foreign aid allocations, and policy priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link coverage spikes to aid flows and policy debates (cite studies on disaster reporting driving aid); examine mechanisms (CNN effect, bureaucratic responsiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue attention cycles and public arenas dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use theoretical models (Anthony Downs' 'Issue Attention Cycle' and 'Public Arenas' model) to interpret patterns of rising and falling media attention and competition among issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these models to explain limited windows of attention, competition for public salience, and the movement of climate change across arenas over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative content-analysis methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ rigorous content-analytic methods across outlets and countries (headline coding, page placement, source coding, frame coding, longitudinal counts) for systematic comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow replication-friendly coding schemes, sample comparable outlets across countries, and report coding protocols; examples include multi-country analyses of forty English-language newspapers across 17 countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of solution-oriented versus threat-oriented coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess balance between stories that present solutions/policy options (renewable energy, mitigation strategies, adaptation measures) and those that emphasize threats/catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify presence of solution frames and evaluate whether reporting moves audiences toward actionable responses or only highlights problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language choices and sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate word choices and rhetorical strategies that may 'transform uncertainties into a sequence of events leading to catastrophe', increasing sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify sensationalist headlines and alarmist sequences; assess their effects on perceived urgency versus anxiety and policy response.
